bib.title: TableRAG: A Retrieval Augmented Generation Framework for Heterogeneous Document Reasoning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "TableRAG: A Retrieval Augmented Generation Framework for Heterogeneous Document Reasoning", Xiaohan Yu, Pu Jian, Chong Chen (Huawei Cloud BU, Beijing). The text says arXiv:2506.10380v2 [cs.CL], 30 Sep 2025. No venue is printed, so treat it as a preprint, 2025. Code: github.com/yxh-y/TableRAG.

COVERAGE: All 20 of 20 pages read, 61,692 of 61,692 chars, including the appendices, Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5, the limitations section and the prompts. I skimmed the references for origins. The figures (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11) are charts with no extracted numbers. I did not open the images, so readings from them are not available.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Flattening tables to Markdown and chunking loses structure and the global view. The authors name this as the failure of standard RAG on documents that mix text and tables.
  number: none
  setup: argued in the introduction, backed by the NaiveRAG baseline (Table 1) and the Figure 1 example.
  quote: "Structural Information Loss: The tabular structure integrity is compromised, leading to information loss or irrelevant context" and "Lack of Global View: Due to document fragmentation, the RAG system struggles with multi-hop global queries"
  where: p.1

- TableRAG beats NaiveRAG, ReAct and TableGPT2 on HybridQA and HeteQA. On WikiTQ the margin over NaiveRAG is small.
  number: HybridQA 47.87 (Claude-3.5), 47.87 (DeepSeek-V3), 48.52 (Qwen); HeteQA overall 44.19, 44.85, 38.82; WikiTQ 84.62, 80.40, 78.00.
  setup: LLM-as-judge accuracy, judged by Qwen-2.5-72B with a 0/1 score. HybridQA is restricted to tables with more than 100 cells. Baselines use the same chunking and retrieval settings.
  quote: "TableRAG Claude-3.5 47.8784.62 44.9440.74 44.19", "DeepSeek-V3 47.87 80.40 43.3251.85 44.85", "Qwen-2.5-72b 48.5278.00 37.65 43.96 38.82"
  where: Table 1, p.6
  Comparison rows (HybridQA / WikiTQ / HeteQA overall):
    - NaiveRAG Claude-3.5: 20.28 / 82.60 / 34.54
    - NaiveRAG DeepSeek-V3: 26.56 / 75.40 / 35.85
    - ReAct Claude-3.5: 43.38 / 69.81 / 29.60
    - TableGPT2: 9.51 / 63.40 / 32.24
  Check the authors' "at least 10% improvement" claim yourself. It holds on HeteQA, where the gain is about 9 points absolute over NaiveRAG. It does not hold on WikiTQ for Claude (84.62 vs NaiveRAG 82.60). The wording is "surpasses all baselines, achieving at least a 10% improvement over the strongest alternative", p.6. The extracted Claude row repeats 47.87 for HybridQA, the same value as DeepSeek-V3. It may be a typo or a column-merge artifact.

- Plain RAG over linearized tables does well on single-source table lookups but poorly on HybridQA and multi-source questions.
  number: NaiveRAG HybridQA 20.28 / 26.56 / 22.62; WikiTQ 82.60 / 75.40 / 66.33.
  setup: same as Table 1.
  quote: "NaiveRAG Claude-3.5 20.28 82.60 33.20 40.35 34.54"
  where: Table 1

- ReAct decomposes too much. It does worse than NaiveRAG on single-source HeteQA but better on multi-source.
  number: ReAct HeteQA single-source 26.40 (Claude), against NaiveRAG 33.20.
  setup: Table 1.
  quote: "Queries that could be resolved with single SQL execution are instead decomposed into multiple subqueries. This over-fragmentation may introduce errors or incomplete information"
  where: §5.2, p.6

- Ablation: document retrieval matters most on HybridQA and SQL execution matters most on HeteQA. Dropping context-aware decomposition, SQL execution or document retrieval each lowers the score.
  number: none in the text. The numbers are in the Figure 4 chart.
  setup: DeepSeek-V3 backbone.
  quote: "On HybridQA, document retrieval proves particularly critical... for HeteQA, SQL execution proves more influential"
  where: §5.3, p.7

- Execution is more efficient than ReAct's. TableRAG needs fewer steps but costs more wall-clock time.
  number: 63.55% resolved in fewer than five steps, plus 30.00% in exactly five. Latency (s), ReAct vs TableRAG: WikiTQ total 13.50 vs 17.70, per step 5.92 vs 7.93; HeteQA total 24.57 vs 45.65, per step 7.70 vs 10.79.
  setup: Qwen-72B-Instruct backbone for the latency test; max 5 iterations.
  quote: "resolving approximately 63.55% of instances in fewer than five steps and an additional 30.00% precisely within five"
  where: §6.1, p.7; Table 2
  Conflict: the text says "TableRAG incurs lower latency compared to ReAct", but Table 2 shows TableRAG with higher latency on every column. Do not repeat the text claim. Quote the table.

- TableRAG has the lowest failure rate of the methods in the error analysis, with errors split into reasoning errors and refusals or exceeding the iteration limit.
  number: none in the text (Figure 6 is a chart).
  setup: HeteQA, DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen backbones.
  quote: "TableRAG demonstrates the lowest failure rate among the methodologies assessed."
  where: §7.1, p.7

- Exact-match results show smaller and less consistent gains on HybridQA.
  number: TableRAG exact match on HybridQA 42.6 (Claude), 33.1 (DeepSeek-V3), 44.6 (Qwen). ReAct gets 35.4 on DeepSeek-V3, which is higher than TableRAG's 33.1.
  setup: Table 4, exact match.
  quote: "TableRAG Claude-3.5 42.6 86.4 27.8"
  where: Table 4, p.14

- Top-k sensitivity: k=3 was chosen as a balance between accuracy and context length. HybridQA does better at larger k, which the authors attribute to duplicate tables and documents contributing useful overlap.
  number: k tested over {1, 3, 5}; main experiments use k=3.
  setup: DeepSeek-V3, HeteQA and HybridQA, Figure 11.
  quote: "setting k= 3 strikes an effective balance, yielding robust performance across both benchmarks while maintaining computational efficiency."
  where: App. E.2, p.15

- Against other table methods, TableRAG beats TAP4LLM and H-Star. The authors read this as agentic frameworks beating pipeline-style ones.
  number: WikiTQ ReAct 53.80, TableRAG 78.00, H-Star 67.35. HybridQA ReAct 37.38, TableRAG 48.52, TAP4LLM 23.28.
  setup: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct backend.
  quote: "TAP4LLM - 23.28", "H-Star 67.35 -"
  where: Table 5, p.14

- HeteQA benchmark.
  number: 304 examples, 9 domains (the text says 9, the Figure 3 legend lists 8), 136 tables, 5314 wiki entities, 82% single-source and 18% multi-source. Table filter: at least 20 rows and 7 columns, which cut 15,314 tables to 1,345 candidates and then 155 after schema dedup. The text says 136 tables in §4.2 and 155 in App. A.1, with no reconciliation.
  setup: built from the HybridQA Wikipedia tables. Claude-3.7-Sonnet generates queries with SQL and Python, then two annotators verify.
  quote: "we construct 304 high-quality examples whose answers are grounded in both single-source (82%) and multi-source (18%). The resulting benchmark spans 136 distinct tables and 5314 wiki knowledge entities."
  where: §4.2, p.5

- Retrieval settings.
  number: BGE-M3 embeddings; top 30 recalled, top 3 kept after reranking; chunks of 1000 tokens with 200 overlap; at most 5 iterations; backbones Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-2.5-72B.
  quote: "During recall, we retain the top 30 candidates, from which the top 3 are subsequently selected via reranking." and "segments of 1000 tokens, with a 200-token overlap"
  where: §5.1.2, p.5

- Method design.
  number: none
  setup: Offline stage: tables go both into a relational database (MySQL) and, rendered as Markdown, into the text index. Each table chunk is mapped to a table schema (name, columns, type, examples). Online stage loops over four steps: query decomposition, text retrieval (cosine recall then rerank), SQL generation and execution (run only when a retrieved chunk comes from a table), and intermediate answer generation that cross-checks the SQL result against the retrieved text. If the offline step fails, the system falls back to the text-only Markdown path.
  quote: "If the set St is empty, this module is passed." and "TableRAG bypasses the SQL execution pathway and leverages the text retrieval module to extract and reason over markdown-formatted table content."
  where: §3.2–3.3, p.3–4; App. C.3, p.13

LIMITS
- Authors concede: results depend on high-capacity LLMs ("Smaller models that lack specialized instruction tuning may exhibit a marked degradation in performance") and HeteQA is English only.
- Not shown: no smaller-model results, no multilingual results, no cost in tokens or dollars, and no retrieval-only metrics such as recall. SQL correctness is not scored independently of the final answer.
- The judge model (Qwen-2.5-72B) is also one of the tested backbones. No judge-agreement check is reported.
- HeteQA queries and SQL were generated by an LLM from table schemas and then human-verified. The questions favor SQL-shaped operations, which may favor the method. The authors built both the benchmark and the method.
- Single runs. There are no seeds, variances or significance tests.
- Wikipedia tables only. Real enterprise spreadsheets and PDFs are not tested, and tables are assumed extractable into a relational schema.
- The paper is internally inconsistent in places: the latency claim against Table 2, the table count (136 vs 155), and the domain count (9 vs 8).
- Latency is higher than ReAct's in the table, so TableRAG is not cheaper per query than its closest baseline.

BUILDS ON
- RAG: Lewis et al. 2020; Gao et al. 2023 (survey); Borgeaud et al. 2022; Guu et al. 2020.
- Adaptive retrieval: Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2023); RQ-RAG (Chan et al. 2024).
- Global-query motivation: Edge et al. 2024 (GraphRAG).
- Retriever: BGE-M3 (Chen et al. 2024a).
- Benchmarks: HybridQA (Chen et al. 2020); WikiTableQuestions (Pasupat and Liang 2015).
- Baselines: ReAct (Yao et al. 2023); TableGPT2 (Su et al. 2024); TAP4LLM; H-Star.
- Table reasoning: Tab-CoT (Jin and Lu 2023); Chain-of-Table (Wang et al. 2024); Tabsqlify (Nahid and Rafiei 2024); DATER (Ye et al. 2023a); BINDER (Cheng et al. 2022); ReAcTable (Zhang et al. 2023b); InfiAgent-DABench (Hu et al. 2024).
- SQL over Python: PyTond (Shahrokhi et al. 2024), cited for Python overhead on large data.

CODE
- Table schema template (§3.2, p.3): `{"table_name": "<Table Name>", "columns": [["<ColName>", "<Type>", "<Examples>"], ...]}`
- Reconciliation prompt (App. G, p.19): "if the answers are same, you may directly output the answer. If the SQL shows error... try to answer solely based on Content 1. If the two material shows conflict, carefully evaluate both sources, explain the discrepancy, and provide your best assessment."
- Decomposition prompt (App. G, p.18): "If a query can be answered by table content, do not decompose it. And directly put the origin query into the 'solve_subquery' tool." and "Generate exactly ONE subquery at a time."
- Offline preprocessing (App. C.3, p.13): missing-value imputation, column type inference from value consistency, and representative sample selection with length control and value diversity.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): the same question answered by plain RAG, which computes over the top-N chunks and gets 50%, and by TableRAG, which gets 20%. It shows the failure mode in one picture.
- Fig 2 (p.3): offline and online TableRAG architecture, with the table-chunk-to-schema mapping and the branch on whether any top-N result is a table chunk.
- Fig 4 (p.6): ablation bars on HybridQA and HeteQA. The values are not in the text.
- Fig 5 (p.7): distribution of execution steps for TableRAG, ReAct and TableGPT2 on HeteQA.
- Fig 6 (p.8): error breakdown into correct, reasoning error, and refusal or exceeded iterations.
- Fig 11 (p.15): top-k 1, 3, 5 against accuracy.

PROBLEMS
- The Table 1 extraction fuses some cells ("47.8784.62", "44.9440.74"). I split them by column order, and the split is consistent with the other rows.
- The Table 1 header is mangled. The columns are inferred as HybridQA, WikiTQ, and HeteQA split into single-source, multi-source and overall. For the TableRAG Claude row, the overall 44.19 sits between the single-source 44.94 and multi-source 40.74 values, so it is plausible.
- The Table 1 Direct rows have no TableRAG-style single/multi split. For DeepSeek-R1 the single-source value is 3.40 and the multi-source value is 13.46, which looks odd, and the cause is not verified.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
- The paper's own Table 1 header text is "Single-Source Multi-Source Overall".
